cells.tense: You are sitting with what someone is going through right now, and your own feet are still under you.
cells.ask: Offer one person help with the thing they actually asked about, not the bigger thing you can see behind it, and stop when it's done.
cells.core:
You have a practice of being with people, and it's holding. You can sit with what someone is carrying without climbing inside it, which is harder than either half alone. The work you've put into yourself is coming through as steadiness, not as advice.
Your care has a floor under it, and the floor is your own. Right now that's mostly where it is. You can hold someone's hard thing and still know the room you're standing in. Care like this doesn't cost you the way it used to, and the next piece of that same contact is yours to take or let pass — offered on a day that's already full.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold someone's hard thing and still stand in your own room.
cells.verb: feeling with another person, without losing your own edge in it
cells.place: a practice room you keep for yourself

cells.tense: You will be carrying what they might need before they have said a word, and you are already bracing for it.
cells.ask: Pick one person you've been bracing for and do nothing for them today, not even the small thing; if it comes up, you can say why.
cells.core:
You're solving people ahead of time. Before anyone has asked, you've already taken on the shape of their answer — and the steady practice you built for yourself has turned into gear for loads that aren't yours yet. Nothing here is invented. It's just running ahead of the room.
Feeling with someone means you can tell where their day stops and yours starts. Now the two are running together, and you're doing the work of two people to keep up. Letting a load sit with its owner for a day is not withdrawal. It's the same practice, aimed differently — one small act, done once, then you watch what actually happens instead of what you were braced for.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying weight nobody handed you yet.

cells.tense: You had something you felt with people once, and you set it down at a door behind you.
cells.ask: Write down three things you know about one person in your life — from memory, no looking it up — and tell them one of them this week.
cells.core:
You're reliable, and the practice that got you there asks for less contact than it used to. Feeling the room made it harder to do what you had to do, so you stopped letting it in, and the work still got done. People get your effort and not much else.
A technique won't cover this gap; contact will. Compassion here looks like knowing one person well enough to be wrong about them out loud, and that starts small. Pushing feeling back into this won't work. What does is keeping the room you already keep, doing one concrete thing that requires you to have noticed someone first, and seeing what comes of it. Three things about one person, written down, is enough of a start.

cells.tense: You are being gentle with people right now and calling it nothing at all.
cells.ask: Say one sentence out loud to a person — not in your head — about why you kept a practice you've been keeping quietly, and don't explain it afterward.
cells.core:
You keep a practice most people don't see, and it has made you easier to be around than you'd admit. You'll go quiet in an argument, you'll remember the small thing, you'll hold a hard week without mentioning it. People stay close. You'd call the same behavior practical.
The practice has its own shape, and you can say what it is: you've been keeping a light on for other people, one small act at a time, for longer than you'd guess. Naming one act of care, aloud, in your own words, is not bragging and not a confession. It's just the record catching up with what your hands have been doing.
cells.sheetLine: The care is already in the room. You haven't said so.

attempts.check: The record does not say people actually feel this person's care while the person feels nothing — that's a description of the pattern from outside, so the Too Little and Unacknowledged cells must locate the person without asserting what they feel or what anyone else feels. A reader could reasonably say 'I do feel things, I just practice alone,' so the cells stay on what the practice is doing rather than on what the person is. The asks survive a wrong read because each one is one visible act with a finish, useful on its own. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line that tells them what they feel; that gets cut.
